passages.source_text: καὶ ὁ πατὴρ Πολλὰ φαίνῃ μοι εὔλογα λέγων. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Τί οὖν ἔστιν τὸ κρατοῦν σε μὴ εἰς τὴν ἡμετέραν πίστιν ἐλθεῖν, λέγε, ἵνα εἰς αὐτὸ λέγειν ἀρξώμεθα. πολλὰ γάρ ἐστιν τὰ κρατοῦντα· τοὺς μὲν πεπεισμένους ἀσχολίαι ἀγορασμῶν, πράξεων, γεωργιῶν, φροντίδων καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα· ἀπιστοῦσι δὲ (ἀφ’ ὧν εἶ καὶ σύ) ὑπολήψεις τοῦ νομίζειν ἢ θεοὺς τοὺς οὐκ ὄντας εἶναι ἢ τὸ γενέσει τὰ πάντα ὑποκεῖσθαι ἢ αὐτοματισμῷ ἢ τὰς ψυχὰς θνητὰς ἢ καὶ τὸν ἡμέτερον λόγον ψευδῆ ὡς οὐκ οὔσης προνοίας.

ἐγὼ δὲ προνοίᾳ θεοῦ τὰ πάντα διοικεῖσθαι ἐκ τῶν περὶ σὲ γενομένων εἶναι λέγω, τοῦ τοσούτοις ἔτεσιν τὴν διάστασιν σοῦ τε καὶ τῶν σῶν γενέσθαι. ἐπεὶ γὰρ σὺν σοὶ ὄντες ἴσως τῶν τῆς θεοσεβείας λόγων οὐκ ἂν ἐπήκουσαν, ᾠκονομήθη σὺν μητρὶ ἡ ἀποδημία καὶ ναυφραγίῳ καὶ θανάτου ὑπονοίᾳ καὶ ἀπαρτίᾳ, ἔτι τε καὶ ἐκπαιδευθῆναι αὐτοὺς τὰ Ἑλλήνων καὶ ἄθεα δόγματα, ἵνα μᾶλλον ὡς εἰδότες ταῦτα ἀνασκευάζειν δυνατοὶ ὦσιν — ἐπὶ τούτοις τὸ φιλῆσαι τὸν τῆς θεοσεβείας λόγον καὶ ἐμοὶ ἑνωθῆναι δυνηθῆναι πρὸς τὸ συλλαβέσθαι μου τῷ κηρύγματι — ἀλλ’ ἔτι μὴν συνελθεῖν καὶ τὸν ἀδελφὸν Κλήμεντα καὶ οὕτως τὴν μητέρα ἐπιγνωσθῆναι καὶ ὑπὸ θεραπείας τὴν θεότητα πληροφορηθῆναι — καὶ μετ’ οὐ πολὺ εὐθὺ τὰ δίδυμα τέκνα ἐπιγνωσθέντα καὶ ἐπιγνόντα καὶ τῆς ἄλλης ἡμέρας σοὶ συντυχεῖν καὶ τοὺς σοὺς ἀπολαβεῖν. τοσαύτην οὖν ταχεῖαν ἁρμονίαν πανταχόθεν συνδραμοῦσαν εἰς ἕνα γνώμης σκοπὸν οὐκ οἶμαι ἀπρονόητον εἶναι.

καὶ ὁ πατὴρ τῷ Πέτρῳ ἤρξατο λέγειν Μὴ νόμιζε, φίλτατέ μοι Πέτρε, ἐν ἐννοίᾳ μὴ ἔχειν περὶ τοῦ ὑπὸ σοῦ κηρυσσομένου λόγου. πέρας γοῦν ταύτης τῆς παρῳχηκυίας νυκτὸς πολλὰ τοῦ Κλήμεντος προτρεπομένου με τῇ ὑπὸ σοῦ κηρυσσομένῃ ἀληθείᾳ συνθέσθαι, ἀπεκρινάμην Τί γὰρ καινότερον ἐντέλλεσθαι δύναταί τις παρ’ ὃ οἱ ἀρχαῖοι παρῄνεσαν; ὁ δὲ ἠρέμα γελάσας ἔφη Πολλὴ διαφορά, πάτερ, μεταξὺ τῶν τῆς θεοσεβείας λόγων καὶ τῶν τῆς φιλοσοφίας. ὁ γὰρ τῆς ἀληθείας λόγος ἀπόδειξιν ἔχει τὴν ἐκ προφητείας, ὁ δὲ τῆς φιλοσοφίας καλλιλογίας παρέχων ἐκ στοχασμῶν δοκεῖ παριστᾶν τὰς ἀποδείξεις. καὶ ὁμῶς ταῦτα εἰπὼν δείγματος χάριν τὸν περὶ φιλανθρωπίας μοι ἐξέθετο λόγον, ὅνπερ αὐτῷ ὑφηγήσω, ὃς ἀδικώτατός μοι μᾶλλον ἐφαίνετο. καὶ τὸ πῶς ἐρῶ. δίκαιον ἔφασκεν εἶναι καὶ τῷ τύπτοντι αὐτοῦ τὴν σιαγόνα παρατιθέναι καὶ τὴν ἑτέραν, καὶ τῷ αἴροντι αὐτοῦ τὸ ἱμάτιον προσδιδόναι καὶ τὸ μαφόριον, ἀγγαρεύοντι δὲ μίλιον ἓν συναπέρχεσθαι δύο, καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα.

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἀπεκρίνατο Ἀλλ’ ἐνόμισας ἄδικον ὅ,τι δικαιότατόν ἐστιν. εἴ σοι φίλον ἐστίν, ἄκουσον. καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἔφη Πάνυ μοι φίλον. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Οὐ δοκεῖ σοι, δύο ἐχθρῶν βασιλέων ὄντων καὶ διῃρημένας τὰς χώρας ἐχόντων, εἴ τις ἐκ τῶν τοῦ ἑνὸς ὑπηκόων ἐν τῇ τοῦ ἑτέρου χώρᾳ φωραθείη καὶ διὰ τοῦτο θάνατον ὀφειληκώς, ἐὰν ῥαπίσματι καὶ μὴ θανάτῳ τῆς τιμωρίας ἀπολυθῇ, οὐ φαίνεται μὴν ὁ ἀπολύσας φιλάνθρωπος εἶναι; καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἔφη Καὶ πάνυ. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Τί δέ; εἰ καὶ ἴδιόν τι τινὸς αὐτὸς οὗτος ἀφέληται ἢ καὶ ἀλλότριον, ἐπὶ τούτῳ συλληφθεὶς ἐὰν διπλάσιον δῷ, τετραπλάσιον ὀφειληκὼς καὶ τὸ θανεῖν, ὡς ἐν τοῖς τοῦ ἐναντίου ἁλοὺς ὅροις: οὐ δοκεῖ σοι ὅτι ὁ λαβὼν τὸ διπλάσιον· καὶ θανάτου αὐτὸν ἀπολύσας φιλάνθρωπος τυγχάνει; καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἔφη Φαίνεται. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Τί δέ; οὐ χρὴ τὸν ἐν ἑτέρου βασιλείᾳ ὄντα, καὶ ταῦτα πονηροῦ τινὸς ἐχθροῦ, τοῦ ζῆν χάριν πάντας κολακεύειν καὶ ἀγγαρεύουσιν ἐπὶ πλεῖον ὑπείκειν, μὴ προσαγορεύοντας προσαγορεύειν, ἐχθροὺς διαλλάσσειν, ὀργιζομένοις μὴ φιλονεικεῖν, τὰ ἑαυτοῦ ἀδεῶς παντὶ αἰτοῦντι παρέχειν, καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα; καὶ ὁ πατὴρ Πάντα μᾶλλον εὐλόγως ὑποσταίην, εἴπερ τούτων τὸ ζῆν προκρίνει.

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Οὔκουν οὓς ἀδικεῖσθαι ἔλεγες, αὐτοὶ παρορισταὶ τυγχάνουσιν, καθὰ ἐν ἑτέρου εἰσὶν βασιλείᾳ, καὶ τοσοῦτον πλεονέκται εἰσίν, ὅσον κεκτημένοι ὦσιν; οἱ δ᾽ ἀδικεῖν νομιζόμενοι τοσαῦτα ἑκάστῳ τῷ ἐξ ἐναντίας ὄντι χαρίζονται, ὅσα ἂν αὐτοῖς ἔχειν συγχωρῶσιν. αὐτῶν γάρ ἐστιν ταῦτα τῶν τὰ παρόντα ἑλομένων. καὶ εἰς τοσοῦτον φιλάνθρωποί εἰσιν, ὡς τὸ ζῆν αὐτοῖς συγχωρεῖν. καὶ τὸ μὲν παράδειγμα οὕτως ἔχει, ἄκουε δὴ αὐτὸ τὸ πρᾶγμα. ὁ τῆς ἀληθείας προφήτης παρὼν ἐδίδαξεν ἡμᾶς ὅτι ὁ τῶν ὅλων δημιουργὸς καὶ θεὸς δυσίν τισιν ἀπένειμεν· βασιλείας δύο, ἀγαθῷ τε καὶ πονηρῷ, δοὺς τῷ μὲν κακῷ τοῦ παρόντος κόσμου μετὰ νόμου τὴν βασιλείαν, ὥστ᾽ ἂν ἔχειν ἐξουσίαν κολάζειν τοὺς ἀδικοῦντας — τῷ δὲ ἀγαθῷ τὸν ἐσόμενον ἀΐδιον αἰῶνα. ἕκαστον δὲ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐλεύθερον ἐποίησεν ἔχειν τὴν ἐξουσίαν ἑαυτὸν ἀπονέμειν ᾧ βούλεται, ἢ τῷ παρόντι κακῷ ἢ τῷ μέλλοντι ἀγαθῷ. ὧν οἱ ἑλόμενοι τὰ παρόντα ἐξουσίαν ἔχουσιν πλουτεῖν, τρυφᾶν, ἥδεσθαι, καὶ πᾶν ὅ,τι ἂν δύνωνται· τῶν γὰρ ἐσομένων ἀγαθῶν οὐδὲν ἔξουσιν. οἱ δὲ τὰ τῆς μελλούσης βασιλείας κρίναντες λαβεῖν τῶν ἐνταῦθα ὡς ἀλλοτρίου βασιλέως ἴδια ὄντα αὐτοῖς νομίζεσθαι οὐκ ἔξεστιν ἢ ὕδατος μόνου καὶ ἄρτου καὶ τούτων μετὰ ἱδρώτων ποριζομένων πρὸς τὸ ζῆν (ἐπειδὴ ἑκοντὶ ἀποθανεῖν οὐκ ἔξεστιν), ἔτι δὲ καὶ περιβολαίου ἑνός· γυμνὸν γὰρ ἑστάναι οὐκ ἐφίεται ἕνεκεν τοῦ πάντ᾽ ἐφορῶντος οὐρανοῦ.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: Our father said, ‘You seem to me to be saying many reasonable things.’ Peter said, ‘Tell me, then, what is holding you back from coming to our faith, so that we may begin to speak directly to it. There are many things that hold people back. For those already convinced, there are the demands of purchases, business, farming, anxieties, and things of that sort. For unbelievers, among whom you too belong, there are assumptions: thinking that gods who do not exist do exist, or that everything is subject to birth-fate or to chance, or that souls are mortal, or that our message is false because there is no providence.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: γενέσει τὰ πάντα ὑποκεῖσθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: everything is subject to birth-fate
lexical_decisions.rationale: Genesis here can denote the determining configuration or fate associated with birth, as distinguished from chance in the next alternative. Birth-fate keeps the birth wording visible; fate determined by the stars at birth is a fuller contextual alternative, but stars are not expressly named in this clause.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτοματισμῷ
lexical_decisions.chosen: chance
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun refers to spontaneous occurrence without directing providence. It is not rendered automation, a misleading modern technical association.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀσχολίαι ἀγορασμῶν, πράξεων, γεωργιῶν, φροντίδων
lexical_decisions.chosen: the demands of purchases, business, farming, anxieties
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural occupations or lack of leisure is the governing idea, and all four listed sources of preoccupation are retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἢ θεοὺς τοὺς οὐκ ὄντας εἶναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: thinking that gods who do not exist do exist
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes the substantivized not-being expression existentially, so that the error concerns treating nonexistent gods as existent. This follows the explicit being/not-being contrast in the phrase. A material predicative alternative is thinking that those who are not gods are gods, which denies their divinity rather than their existence. The main text does not claim that the existential attachment is unique.

passages.text: ‘But I say that everything is governed by God's providence, judging from what has happened to you: your separation from your family for so many years. Since, if they had remained with you, perhaps they would not have listened to the teachings of reverence for God, their journey abroad with their mother was arranged, along with shipwreck, presumed death, and loss of contact. So too was their education in Greek and godless doctrines, so that, knowing them, they might be better able to refute them. After this came their love for the teaching of reverence for God and their ability to join me in helping my proclamation; then their brother Clement's coming together with us, and thus their mother's being recognized and becoming fully convinced of the divinity through healing. Shortly afterward came the twins' being recognized and recognizing in turn, and, on the following day, meeting you and your recovering your family. I do not think that so great and swift a harmony, converging from every direction upon one intended aim, is without providence.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ναυφραγίῳ καὶ θανάτου ὑπονοίᾳ καὶ ἀπαρτίᾳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: along with shipwreck, presumed death, and loss of contact
lexical_decisions.rationale: The list describes the circumstances of the family separation. Ἀπαρτία is read as absence of news or contact in this context; the translation does not supply a particular duration beyond the previously stated years.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ οὕτως τὴν μητέρα ἐπιγνωσθῆναι καὶ ὑπὸ θεραπείας τὴν θεότητα πληροφορηθῆναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: and thus their mother's being recognized and becoming fully convinced of the divinity through healing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text continues the mother as the inferred subject of the second passive infinitive and takes the accusative divinity as the content of her conviction. That connects her recognition with her resulting assurance. A material alternative takes divinity as the expressed accusative subject of that infinitive, parallel to mother as subject of the first: and the divinity was fully confirmed through healing. Neither reading establishes whose divinity is meant, and the English does not identify Peter or the mother as divine.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ δίδυμα τέκνα ἐπιγνωσθέντα καὶ ἐπιγνόντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the twins' being recognized and recognizing in turn
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both passive and active recognition are retained. The unexpressed object of their recognition is not replaced by an invented named person in this clause.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς ἕνα γνώμης σκοπὸν
lexical_decisions.chosen: upon one intended aim
lexical_decisions.rationale: The convergence is toward one aim of intention or purpose. Agreement of belief is a possible contextual emphasis for γνώμη, but the preceding arrangement of events favors an intended aim without naming a separate planner in this phrase.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοσαύτην οὖν ταχεῖαν ἁρμονίαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: so great and swift a harmony
lexical_decisions.rationale: The degree of magnitude expressed by τοσαύτην is distinguished from the speed expressed by ταχεῖαν, rather than collapsing both into so swift.

passages.text: Our father began to say to Peter, ‘Do not suppose, my dearest Peter, that I have not been thinking about the message you proclaim. Indeed, at the end of this past night, when Clement urged me at length to agree with the truth you proclaim, I answered, “What newer instruction can anyone give beyond what the ancients advised?” He smiled gently and said, “There is a great difference, father, between the teachings of reverence for God and those of philosophy. For the message of truth has its proof from prophecy, whereas the teaching of philosophy offers fine language and seems to present its proofs from conjectures.” Having said this, however, he set out for me, as an example, the teaching about love for humanity that you had explained to him. It seemed to me, rather, utterly unjust. I will tell you how. He said that it was just for someone to offer the other cheek as well to the person striking his cheek; to give his head-covering too to the person taking his cloak; to go two miles with the person compelling him to go one; and other things of this sort.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ δὲ τῆς φιλοσοφίας καλλιλογίας παρέχων ἐκ στοχασμῶν δοκεῖ παριστᾶν τὰς ἀποδείξεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: the teaching of philosophy offers fine language and seems to present its proofs from conjectures
lexical_decisions.rationale: The favorable-sounding language and the qualification seems are retained alongside the criticism of conjectural proofs. The translation does not replace conjecture by observation or prophecy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν περὶ φιλανθρωπίας μοι ἐξέθετο λόγον
lexical_decisions.chosen: he set out for me ... the teaching about love for humanity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term is a broad humane love or kindness toward human beings. Love for humanity keeps its human object explicit and connects it with the ensuing discussion of humane treatment.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ μαφόριον
lexical_decisions.chosen: his head-covering
lexical_decisions.rationale: The garment can be a scarf, kerchief, or head-covering. It is distinguished from the cloak named immediately before it, rather than replaced by the tunic familiar from another form of the saying.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ὁμῶς ταῦτα εἰπὼν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Having said this, however
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verified selected print reads ὁμῶς, not the usual adversative accentuation ὅμως. The main text interprets the continuation adversatively: after contrasting the two teachings he nevertheless gives the example. Non-adversative alike or together is a lexical alternative for the printed form. This interpretation is not a change to the source or a claim that the Greek has been normalized to ὅμως.

passages.text: Peter answered, ‘But you judged unjust what is most just. If you wish, listen.’ The father said, ‘I very much wish to.’ Peter said, ‘Suppose there are two hostile kings, each with a separate territory. If one king's subject is discovered in the other's country and thereby owes death, but is released from punishment with a slap rather than death, does not the one who released him appear humane?’ The father said, ‘Very much so.’ Peter said, ‘What, then, if this same man takes from someone something of that person's own, or even something belonging to someone else, and is caught for it? If he gives double, although he owes fourfold and death because he was caught within the enemy's borders, does it not seem to you that the one who took double and released him from death is humane?’ The father said, ‘It appears so.’ Peter said, ‘What then? Should not someone in another's kingdom, and that of a wicked enemy at that, for the sake of staying alive, flatter everyone, yield beyond what is demanded by those who compel service, greet those who do not greet him, reconcile enemies, avoid quarreling with angry people, freely provide his possessions to everyone who asks, and do other things of this sort?’ The father said, ‘I would all the more reasonably endure everything, if indeed he puts staying alive before these things.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἴδιόν τι τινὸς αὐτὸς οὗτος ἀφέληται ἢ καὶ ἀλλότριον
lexical_decisions.chosen: this same man takes from someone something of that person's own, or even something belonging to someone else
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast is read as the victim's own property versus another person's property in the victim's possession. An alternative takes own in relation to the person doing the taking. The main rendering makes the contextual property relations intelligible without changing the two expressed categories into a single generic theft.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀγγαρεύουσιν ἐπὶ πλεῖον ὑπείκειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: yield beyond what is demanded by those who compel service
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb refers to impressed or compulsory service, with yielding to a greater extent. The rendering retains the excess compliance without introducing a specific journey or distance into this general instruction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ ἑαυτοῦ ἀδεῶς παντὶ αἰτοῦντι παρέχειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: freely provide his possessions to everyone who asks
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ἀδεῶς can mean without fear or hesitation. Freely is read as unhesitating willingness, not a claim that the hostile country is safe or that the possessions carry no monetary value.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἴπερ τούτων τὸ ζῆν προκρίνει
lexical_decisions.chosen: if indeed he puts staying alive before these things
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source moves from the father's first-person willingness to an expressed third-person verb. He retains the hypothetical person as its subject rather than silently replacing it with I; the comparison is preference for life over the burdens just listed.

passages.text: Peter said, ‘Is it not, then, the case that those whom you said were being wronged are themselves trespassers, since they are in another's kingdom, and are taking more than their due to the extent that they possess anything? Those thought to be doing wrong grant each person on the opposing side as much as they allow that person to have. For these things belong to those who have chosen the present. They are so humane as even to permit them to live. That is how the illustration stands; now hear the actual matter. When the prophet of truth was present, he taught us that the creator and God of all assigned two kingdoms to two beings, a good one and an evil one. He gave the evil one the kingdom of this present world, together with a law, so that he might have authority to punish wrongdoers; to the good one, the coming eternal age. He made each human being free, with authority to assign himself to whichever he wishes: either the present evil or the future good. Those who have chosen the present have authority to be rich, live luxuriously, enjoy themselves, and do whatever they can, for they will have none of the good things to come. But those who have decided to receive the things of the future kingdom may not consider any of the things here their own, since they belong to another king, except only water and bread—and these obtained with sweat to sustain life, since voluntary death is not permitted—and also a single covering. For one is not allowed to stand naked because of heaven, which sees everything.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτοὶ παρορισταὶ τυγχάνουσιν, καθὰ ἐν ἑτέρου εἰσὶν βασιλείᾳ, καὶ τοσοῦτον πλεονέκται εἰσίν
lexical_decisions.chosen: trespassers ... taking more than their due
lexical_decisions.rationale: These words occur in the clause about being in another's kingdom. The first denotes crossing a boundary, the second grasping or claiming an excessive share. The rendering does not replace their property-based accusation by a general description of sinful attitudes.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δυσίν τισιν ἀπένειμεν· βασιλείας δύο, ἀγαθῷ τε καὶ πονηρῷ
lexical_decisions.chosen: assigned two kingdoms to two beings, a good one and an evil one
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two recipients are distinct from the creator assigning their realms. The English supplies beings for the substantivized adjectives without naming either as a second creator or as a particular named angel.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἢ τῷ παρόντι κακῷ ἢ τῷ μέλλοντι ἀγαθῷ
lexical_decisions.chosen: either the present evil or the future good
lexical_decisions.rationale: These substantivized adjective forms permit reference to the present evil and future good as conditions or realms, alongside the preceding recipients of the kingdoms. The translation retains the broad evil/good antithesis instead of forcing every occurrence to name an individual being; the inflected forms themselves do not settle masculine versus neuter reference.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἕνεκεν τοῦ πάντ᾽ ἐφορῶντος οὐρανοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: because of heaven, which sees everything
lexical_decisions.rationale: Heaven is the expressed all-seeing subject. It may function as a reverential reference to heavenly observation, but the main text does not silently replace it with God or infer a particular observer.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
